title: SQL LEFT JOIN
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and row-preservation behaviour of SQL LEFT JOIN.
Write valid SQLite queries using the join and an explicit ON condition.
Predict the effect of matching, unmatched and one-to-many rows.
Interpret NULL-extended columns and distinguish unmatched rows from matched values.
Recognize SQL dialect and database-version compatibility considerations.

understand.concept: LEFT JOIN preserves every row from the left input. Matching right-side rows are attached; when no right-side row matches, the right-side columns are returned as NULL. Multiple matches still produce multiple result rows.
understand.whyItMatters: It supports reports that must include entities even when related activity is absent, such as customers with no orders or departments with no employees.
understand.analogy: It is like keeping the entire first list and attaching a matching record from the second list when one exists.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not capture row multiplication or the difference between a missing match and a matched row whose value is itself NULL.

examples.title: Create and inspect the sample data
examples.explanation: The left input contains four customers; all four must remain in a LEFT JOIN result.

examples.title: Keep customers even without orders
examples.expectedOutput: Asha Rao | 101; Asha Rao | 102; Bilal Khan | NULL; Chitra Das | 103; Dev Patel | NULL
examples.explanation: Bilal and Dev remain even though no order matches their customer identifiers.

examples.title: Find customers with no matching order
examples.explanation: Testing a non-nullable right-side key for NULL identifies rows with no match.

examples.title: Count orders without counting the placeholder row
examples.expectedOutput: Asha Rao | 2; Bilal Khan | 0; Chitra Das | 1; Dev Patel | 0
examples.explanation: COUNT(o.order_id) ignores the NULL placeholder. COUNT(*) would count one output row even for a customer with no order.

examples.title: Filter matches while preserving customers
examples.expectedOutput: Asha Rao | 101; Bilal Khan | NULL; Chitra Das | NULL; Dev Patel | NULL
examples.explanation: Putting the right-side filter in ON preserves all left rows. Putting it in WHERE would remove rows with no qualifying right-side match.

practise.guidedTask: Run the shared setup and execute each SQL LEFT JOIN example. Before each query, mark which customer and order rows you expect to remain; then compare your prediction with the actual result.
practise.independentTask: Create departments and employees tables with at least five departments and six employees. Include at least one department with no employees and one employee with no department. Write five queries using the join type from this lesson, including one aggregate and one unmatched-row report.
hints: Start by identifying which table must be preserved.
Write the ON predicate using the actual relationship keys.
Add ORDER BY for deterministic output.
Use a non-nullable primary key to detect a missing match.
Check the DBMS version before relying on RIGHT or FULL OUTER JOIN.

options: Every row from the left input
Every row from the left input only
Every row from the right input only
questions.answer: Every row from the left input
questions.explanation: The selected join type determines which unmatched rows remain.

questions.prompt: Where is the relationship between the input rows normally specified?
questions.explanation: ON contains the join predicate that determines matching pairs.

questions.prompt: What can happen when one row matches two rows on the other side?
options: The row can appear twice in the result
The join changes to CROSS JOIN
questions.answer: The row can appear twice in the result
questions.explanation: A join returns matching row pairs, so one-to-many relationships multiply output rows.

questions.prompt: What is a safe way to avoid ambiguous column references?
options: Qualify columns with table names or aliases
Rename every column after the query
questions.answer: Qualify columns with table names or aliases
questions.explanation: Qualified names identify which input supplies a column.

questions.prompt: What should be checked when using this join across database engines?
questions.explanation: Join support and syntax details can vary by engine and version.
